title: Linux Command Line Essentials: From Your First Command to Log-Parsing Pipelines
intro: The Linux command line is a text interface where a program called the shell reads what you type, runs the matching programs, and shows you their output. This lesson teaches you to move around the filesystem, manage and read files, combine small tools with pipes and redirection, and build the grep, cut, sort and uniq pipelines that analysts use to summarize large log files in seconds.

sections.heading: The shell, the prompt, and the shape of a command
sections.content:
A **shell** is a program that reads the text you type, interprets it, and asks the operating system to run other programs on your behalf. Think of a restaurant waiter: you do not walk into the kitchen (the kernel); you give an order in a fixed format and the waiter carries it there and brings back the result. **bash** (Bourne Again SHell) is the default shell on most Linux distributions. Others exist (zsh, dash, fish), and everything in this lesson works in bash. A **terminal** is only the window; the shell is the program running inside it.

When the shell is ready for input it prints a **prompt**:

```
analyst@web01:~/logs$
```

- analyst is the user you are logged in as.
- web01 is the hostname of the machine.
- ~/logs is the current working directory (~ is shorthand for your home directory).
- $ means a normal user. A # at the end means root, the all-powerful account, so slow down when you see it.

Every command follows the same structure:

```
command [options] [arguments]
```

```bash
ls -l /var/log
head -n 5 auth_sample.log
```

The **command** is the program to run. **Options** (also called flags or switches) change how it behaves: short options use one dash (-l), long options use two (--all), and short options can usually be combined (-la means -l -a). Some options take a value, as in -n 5. **Arguments** are the things the command works on, such as a file or directory. The shell splits your line into words on whitespace, which is why a filename containing a space needs quotes. Linux is also case sensitive: Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files.

Every command finishes with an **exit status**, a number the shell stores in the variable $?. Zero means success and anything else means some kind of failure:

```bash
ls /nonexistent
echo $?
```

```
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
2
```

Exit codes are what let you chain commands safely later in this lesson.

### Getting help without leaving the terminal

Nobody memorizes every option. Analysts become fast because they know where to look:

- **man ls** opens the manual page. Press space to page down, / to search, n for the next match, and q to quit. Manual pages are grouped in numbered sections, so man 5 passwd shows the file format while man 1 passwd shows the command.
- **ls --help** prints a short summary straight to the terminal. It works for most GNU tools.
- **apropos copy** (same as man -k copy) searches manual page descriptions when you know what you want but not the command name.
- **type** and **which** tell you what a name actually means:

```bash
type cd
type ls
which grep
```

```
cd is a shell builtin
ls is aliased to 'ls --color=auto'
/usr/bin/grep
```

Builtins like cd live inside the shell and are documented with help cd, not man. Aliases are shortcuts defined in your shell. This matters when a command behaves differently than a colleague's: your ls may be an alias with extra options.

**Habit to build:** before running an unfamiliar command with an unfamiliar option, read its man page for ten seconds. On a production server that habit prevents outages.

sections.heading: Navigating the filesystem: pwd, cd, and ls
sections.content:
Every shell session has a **current working directory**, the place relative paths are measured from. Lose track of it and you will run commands against the wrong files.

```bash
pwd
```

```
/home/analyst/logs
```

**pwd** (print working directory) answers where you are. **cd** (change directory) moves you.

### Absolute versus relative paths

An **absolute path** starts with / and means the same thing no matter where you are: /home/analyst/logs. A **relative path** does not start with / and is resolved from the current directory: logs/archive. Four special symbols make relative navigation fast:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| . | The current directory | ./run.sh runs a script in this directory |
| .. | The parent directory | cd .. goes up one level |
| ~ | Your home directory | cd ~/logs |
| - | The previous directory (with cd) | cd - jumps back and forth |

Typing cd with no argument takes you home. The cd - trick is a huge time saver when you bounce between two distant directories.

```bash
cd /etc/ssh
cd ~/logs
cd -
```

```
/etc/ssh
```

cd - prints the directory it returned to. If a directory name contains a space, quote it: cd 'Incident Reports 2026'.

### Listing with ls

**ls** lists directory contents. Plain ls hides a lot, so these options matter:

- **-l** long format, one entry per line with details
- **-a** all entries, including hidden ones (names starting with a dot)
- **-h** human-readable sizes (4.2K, 18M) when combined with -l
- **-t** sort by modification time, newest first (add **-r** to reverse, so ls -ltr puts the newest file at the bottom, right above your next prompt)
- **-R** recurse into subdirectories
- **-d** show a directory itself instead of its contents

### Reading an ls -l line

```bash
ls -lh
```

```
total 72K
drwxr-xr-x 2 analyst analyst 4.0K Nov  1 17:02 archive
-rw-r--r-- 1 analyst analyst  48K Nov  2 09:15 auth_sample.log
lrwxrwxrwx 1 analyst analyst   15 Nov  2 08:40 latest -> auth_sample.log
```

Read each line left to right:

1. **First character** is the type: - for a regular file, d for a directory, l for a symbolic link.
2. **The next nine characters** are the permission bits. Their meaning is covered in the separate Linux fundamentals lesson; here, just recognize where they sit.
3. **Link count** (how many names point at the data).
4. **Owner** and **group**.
5. **Size** in bytes, or human-readable with -h.
6. **Modification time**. This is a first stop in an investigation: a file changed at 03:00 on a Sunday deserves a question.
7. **Name**. For symlinks, the target follows the arrow.

**Pitfall:** hidden files such as .bash_history and .ssh are invisible to plain ls. When you investigate a home directory, always use ls -la. Attackers know defenders forget this.

sections.heading: Creating, copying, moving, deleting, and linking
sections.content:
These commands change the filesystem, so the cost of a typo is real. Learn what each one does silently.

### touch and mkdir

**touch** creates an empty file if it does not exist, or updates its modification time if it does. **mkdir** creates directories. The **-p** option creates every missing parent and does not complain if the directory already exists, which is what you want in scripts:

```bash
mkdir -p case-0142/evidence/logs
touch case-0142/notes.txt
ls -R case-0142
```

```
case-0142:
evidence  notes.txt

case-0142/evidence:
logs

case-0142/evidence/logs:
```

### cp and mv

**cp source dest** copies a file. Use **-r** (recursive) for directories, **-p** to preserve timestamps and ownership where possible, and **-i** to prompt before overwriting. Without -i, cp overwrites an existing destination with no warning.

**mv source dest** moves a file, and it is also how you rename, because on Linux a rename is just a move within the same directory:

```bash
cp auth_sample.log case-0142/evidence/logs/
mv notes.txt case-0142/notes-initial.txt
```

Like cp, mv silently replaces an existing target. Use **mv -i** (ask first) or **mv -n** (never overwrite). When copying evidence, preserve originals: work on a copy and keep the source untouched.

### rm and the danger of rm -rf

**rm** deletes files. There is no recycle bin and no undo. **rm -r** deletes directories and everything inside them. **-f** suppresses prompts and errors. Combined, **rm -rf** is the most dangerous everyday command in Linux. Real incidents come from the same few mistakes:

- **A stray space:** rm -rf /tmp/work /* instead of rm -rf /tmp/work/* deletes from the root of the filesystem.
- **An empty variable:** rm -rf $DIR/ becomes rm -rf / when DIR is unset.
- **A glob that matches more than you expected.**

Defensive habits: run ls with the exact same arguments first to preview what will match, use rm -i or rm -I (one prompt for bulk deletes) when working by hand, and use rmdir to remove only empty directories. Press Tab to complete paths rather than typing them in full.

### Hard links and symbolic links

A file's name and its data are separate things. The data lives at an **inode**, and a directory entry is a name pointing at it. **ln** creates extra names.

```bash
ln auth_sample.log hard.log
ln -s auth_sample.log soft.log
ls -li
```

```
 262417 -rw-r--r-- 2 analyst analyst 48213 Nov  2 09:15 auth_sample.log
 262417 -rw-r--r-- 2 analyst analyst 48213 Nov  2 09:15 hard.log
 262590 lrwxrwxrwx 1 analyst analyst    15 Nov  2 09:20 soft.log -> auth_sample.log
```

- A **hard link** is a second name for the same inode (same number in the first column). Delete one name and the data survives until the last name is gone. Hard links cannot cross filesystems and cannot point at directories.
- A **symbolic link** (ln -s) is a small file that stores a path, like a shortcut. If the target is deleted or moved, the symlink dangles and points at nothing.

**Why analysts care:** attackers use symlinks to redirect where a program reads or writes, and a quick ls -l shows the arrow that gives it away.

sections.heading: Viewing and reading files
sections.content:
Most investigation work is reading text, so choose the right viewer for the size of the file.

### cat

**cat** (concatenate) prints files to the terminal, one after another. It is ideal for short files. The option **-n** numbers the lines.

```bash
cat -n notes.txt
```

```
     1  Reported by help desk 08:50
     2  Host: web01
     3  Status: triage
```

Never cat a huge log or an unknown binary file: it floods the terminal, and binary data can scramble your terminal settings (the reset command repairs it).

### less

**less** is a pager: it opens a file one screen at a time without loading the whole thing, so it handles multi-gigabyte logs. Its keys are worth memorizing because they are the same ones man uses:

- space / b : page down / page up
- g / G : jump to the start / end of the file
- /pattern : search forward; **n** next match, **N** previous match
- **F** : follow the end of the file as it grows (Ctrl-C to stop following)
- **q** : quit

Start less with **-S** to stop long lines wrapping, which keeps columnar logs readable.

### head and tail

**head** shows the beginning of a file and **tail** the end. The default is 10 lines; **-n** sets the count.

```bash
head -n 3 auth_sample.log
tail -n 2 auth_sample.log
```

```
Nov  2 09:14:03 web01 sshd[2211]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.45 port 51522 ssh2
Nov  2 09:14:05 web01 sshd[2213]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51530 ssh2
Nov  2 09:14:09 web01 sshd[2214]: Failed password for invalid user test from 203.0.113.45 port 51544 ssh2
Nov  2 09:15:41 web01 sshd[2290]: Accepted password for deploy from 198.51.100.7 port 40112 ssh2
Nov  2 09:16:02 web01 sshd[2301]: Failed password for root from 192.0.2.88 port 33901 ssh2
```

The most useful variant is **tail -f**, which keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are appended. That is how you watch a log live while you reproduce a problem or wait for an attacker's next move. Use **tail -F** (capital F) for logs that get rotated, because it re-opens the file when the name is replaced by a new one. Press Ctrl-C to stop.

```bash
tail -F auth_sample.log
```

### wc and file

**wc** (word count) counts lines (-l), words (-w) and bytes (-c). The line count is the one you will use constantly, because one log entry is usually one line:

```bash
wc -l auth_sample.log
```

```
312 auth_sample.log
```

**file** inspects the content of a file and reports its real type, ignoring the extension:

```bash
file report.pdf invoice.docx auth_sample.log
```

```
report.pdf:       PDF document, version 1.7
invoice.docx:     ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64
auth_sample.log:  ASCII text
```

The middle line is the lesson: a file named like a document that is really an executable is a classic red flag. Run file before you open anything you do not trust. For compressed logs, zcat and zless read .gz files without unpacking them.

sections.heading: Wildcards, globbing, and quoting
sections.content:
Typing every filename is slow and error-prone. **Globbing** lets you describe a set of files with a pattern. The crucial fact: **the shell expands the pattern, not the command.** When you type ls *.log, bash replaces *.log with the list of matching names before ls ever starts. ls never sees the asterisk.

### Glob patterns

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|---|---|---|
| * | Any run of characters, including none | *.log matches auth.log and syslog.log |
| ? | Exactly one character | log?.txt matches log1.txt, not log10.txt |
| [abc] | One character from the set | log[123].txt |
| [a-c] | One character from a range | [a-c]*.txt |
| [!abc] | One character not in the set | [!0-9]*.txt |
| [[:digit:]] | A character class (digit, alpha, upper) | access-[[:digit:]].log |

Two behaviors surprise beginners. First, * does not match hidden files (names starting with a dot) unless you ask with .* explicitly. Second, if nothing matches, bash passes the pattern through literally, so ls *.xyz complains about a file named *.xyz.

### Brace expansion

**Braces** generate strings; they do not look at the filesystem at all, so they work for files that do not exist yet:

```bash
mkdir -p case/{logs,notes,evidence}
touch report-{01..03}.txt
echo backup-{mon,tue,wed}
cp auth_sample.log{,.bak}
```

```
backup-mon backup-tue backup-wed
```

The last command expands to cp auth_sample.log auth_sample.log.bak, a handy backup idiom. Zero-padded ranges such as {01..12} produce 01, 02 and so on up to 12.

### Glob versus regular expression

Globs and **regular expressions** (regex) look similar but are different languages used in different places. Globs match filenames and are expanded by the shell. Regex matches text inside data and is interpreted by tools like grep, sed and awk.

| Idea | Glob | Regex |
|---|---|---|
| Any characters | * | .* |
| One character | ? | . |
| Starts with err | err* | ^err |
| Ends with .log | *.log | [.]log$ |

The star is the classic trap: in a glob it means anything, but in regex it means repeat the previous item zero or more times.

### Quoting

Because the shell acts on special characters before the command runs, you need quotes to pass them through untouched:

- **Single quotes** keep everything literal: echo '$HOME *' prints exactly that.
- **Double quotes** stop globbing and word splitting but still expand variables: echo "$HOME" prints /home/analyst.
- **Unquoted** text is expanded, glob-matched and split on spaces.

```bash
grep 'Failed.*root' auth_sample.log
find . -name '*.log'
rm 'old notes.txt'
```

The regex in grep and the pattern in find must be quoted, otherwise the shell tries to glob them first. A related trap: a file whose name begins with a dash, such as one named -rf, looks like an option to rm *. Use rm -- *, or write ./* so every name starts with ./.

sections.heading: Streams, pipes, and redirection
sections.content:
Every Linux program is born with three open **streams**:

- **stdin** (file descriptor 0): input, normally your keyboard
- **stdout** (file descriptor 1): normal output, normally your screen
- **stderr** (file descriptor 2): error and diagnostic messages, also normally your screen

Splitting normal output from errors is a deliberate design. It means you can capture results in a file while errors still reach your eyes, or throw away the noise without losing the data. **Redirection** rewires these streams, and a **pipe** connects the stdout of one program to the stdin of the next.

| Operator | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| cmd > file | Send stdout to file, overwriting it | ls > listing.txt |
| cmd >> file | Append stdout to file | date >> timeline.txt |
| cmd < file | Read stdin from file | sort < ips.txt |
| cmd 2> file | Send stderr to file | find / -name x 2> errors.txt |
| cmd > out 2>&1 | Send stdout and stderr to the same file | make > build.log 2>&1 |
| cmd &> file | Bash shorthand for both streams | make &> build.log |
| cmd 2> /dev/null | Discard error messages | find / -name '*.conf' 2> /dev/null |
| cmd1 \| cmd2 | Pipe stdout of cmd1 into cmd2 | cat auth.log \| wc -l |
| cmd \| tee file | Show output and save it to a file | ls \| tee listing.txt |

**/dev/null** is a special file that accepts everything and stores nothing, the bit bucket. It is the standard way to silence noise, such as the endless Permission denied messages when you search the whole disk as a normal user.

```bash
find / -name '*.conf' 2>/dev/null | head -n 3
```

```
/etc/ssh/ssh_config
/etc/resolv.conf
/etc/host.conf
```

### Order matters in 2>&1

The shell processes redirections left to right. 2>&1 means point stderr at wherever stdout currently points. So write the file redirect first:

```bash
make > build.log 2>&1
```

That sends both streams to build.log. The reverse, make 2>&1 > build.log, first points stderr at the screen and only then moves stdout to the file, so errors still appear on screen.

### The overwrite trap

The operator > truncates the target file to zero length before the command starts. That makes this tempting command destructive:

```bash
sort ips.txt > ips.txt
```

The shell empties ips.txt first, then sort reads an empty file. You lose your data. Write to a different file and rename it, or use sort -o ips.txt ips.txt, which is built to handle this. Setting set -o noclobber makes bash refuse to overwrite existing files with >.

### Pipes and tee

A pipe only carries stdout. Error messages from the left-hand command still go to the terminal unless you redirect them. Pipelines are how small single-purpose tools become powerful: each program does one job and passes text along.

**tee** is a T-junction. It copies its input to the screen and to a file, which lets you save an intermediate result without breaking the pipeline. Use tee -a to append:

```bash
grep 'Failed' auth_sample.log | tee failed.txt | wc -l
```

```
287
```

That saved all 287 failed lines to failed.txt and printed the count.

sections.heading: The analyst's text-processing toolkit
sections.content:
Logs are text, and Linux ships with small tools that each filter, slice, or count text. Learn these seven and you can answer most log questions without any special software.

### grep: find matching lines

**grep** prints lines that match a pattern. The pattern is a regular expression, but plain words work too.

| Flag | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| -i | Ignore case | grep -i failed auth.log |
| -v | Invert: lines that do NOT match | grep -v CRON syslog |
| -r | Recurse through a directory | grep -r 'password' /srv/app |
| -E | Extended regex (adds +, ?, parentheses and alternation) | grep -E 'Failed\|Invalid' auth.log |
| -o | Print only the matching part | grep -o -E '[0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+[.][0-9]+' auth.log |
| -c | Count matching lines | grep -c 'Failed password' auth.log |
| -n | Show line numbers | grep -n Accepted auth.log |
| -l | List only filenames that match | grep -rl 'ssh2' . |

Basic regex building blocks: ^ anchors the start of a line, $ the end, . matches any one character, * repeats the previous item, [0-9] is a set, and [.] matches a literal dot (a dot inside brackets loses its special meaning). With -E you also get + (one or more) and | (alternation). Always single-quote your patterns.

### cut: slice columns

**cut** extracts fields. Use **-d** to set the delimiter and **-f** to pick fields:

```bash
echo 'root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' | cut -d: -f1,7
```

```
root:/bin/bash
```

cut treats every single delimiter as a separator, so it is best for structured files (CSV, passwd-style, logs with exactly one space between fields).

### sort and uniq: rank and count

**sort** orders lines; **-n** sorts numerically, **-r** reverses, **-u** removes duplicates. **uniq** collapses *adjacent* identical lines, and **uniq -c** prefixes each with its count. Because uniq only sees neighbors, you must sort first. The pair sort | uniq -c is the analyst's frequency table.

### awk: field extraction

**awk** splits each line on runs of whitespace and exposes the pieces as $1, $2, and so on. $NF is the last field and $(NF-3) counts back from it. It can also filter:

```bash
awk '{print $1, $3}' auth_sample.log | head -n 2
awk '$6 == "Failed" {print $(NF-3)}' auth_sample.log | head -n 2
```

```
Nov 09:14:03
Nov 09:14:05
203.0.113.45
203.0.113.45
```

Unlike cut -d' ', awk treats a run of spaces as one separator, so it copes with the double space in Nov  2.

### sed and tr: transform text

**sed** is a stream editor. Its workhorse is substitution, s/old/new/, with the **g** suffix to replace every match on a line:

```bash
sed 's/203[.]0[.]113[.]45/REDACTED/g' auth_sample.log | head -n 1
```

```
Nov  2 09:14:03 web01 sshd[2211]: Failed password for root from REDACTED port 51522 ssh2
```

sed prints to stdout and leaves the file untouched. Adding **-i** edits the file in place, so use -i.bak to keep a backup. **tr** translates or deletes single characters: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' uppercases, tr -s ' ' squeezes repeated spaces into one, and tr -d ':' deletes colons. tr reads only stdin, so feed it with a pipe or <.

sections.heading: Worked example: who is hammering the web server?
sections.content:
Suppose a web server's access log is flooded with failed logins and you need the offending IPs now. The file access.log has one request per line with single-space-separated fields: timestamp, client IP, method, path, status code.

```
2026-11-02T09:14:03Z 203.0.113.45 GET /login 401
2026-11-02T09:14:04Z 203.0.113.45 POST /login 401
2026-11-02T09:14:09Z 198.51.100.7 GET /index.html 200
2026-11-02T09:14:11Z 203.0.113.45 POST /login 401
2026-11-02T09:14:15Z 192.0.2.88 POST /login 401
```

### Build it one stage at a time

The right way to build a pipeline is incrementally: run the first stage, look at the output, then add the next. You always know which stage broke something.

**Step 1: how big is the problem?**

```bash
wc -l access.log
grep -c ' 401$' access.log
```

```
18204 access.log
1431
```

The pattern ' 401$' means a space, then 401, at the end of the line. Anchoring avoids matching a 401 elsewhere in the line, such as a path containing it.

**Step 2: keep only failures and extract the IP column.**

```bash
grep ' 401$' access.log | cut -d' ' -f2 | head -n 3
```

```
203.0.113.45
203.0.113.45
203.0.113.45
```

grep selects rows, cut selects a column. That is the whole mental model: filter rows, then slice columns.

**Step 3: count and rank.**

```bash
grep ' 401$' access.log | cut -d' ' -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5
```

```
   1212 203.0.113.45
    201 192.0.2.88
     14 198.51.100.7
      4 10.0.4.17
```

Read it stage by stage:

1. grep keeps only the 401 lines.
2. cut extracts field 2, the IP.
3. sort puts identical IPs next to each other. Without it, uniq would count only adjacent repeats and produce misleading numbers.
4. uniq -c collapses duplicates and prefixes the count.
5. sort -rn orders numerically (-n) with the biggest first (-r). Without -n, 9 would sort after 10 because text order compares character by character.
6. head -n 5 keeps the top five.

### Same idea, other questions

Change one stage and the same template answers a new question. Which paths do those top attackers hit?

```bash
grep '^[^ ]* 203[.]0[.]113[.]45 ' access.log | cut -d' ' -f4 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

Which IPs fail most often in the SSH log? The field count varies because invalid user adds two words, so use awk and count from the end:

```bash
grep 'Failed password' auth_sample.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
```

```
   241 203.0.113.45
    38 192.0.2.88
     8 198.51.100.7
```

Save the result with tee, or redirect the final output to a file for your case notes.

### What the numbers mean

One address responsible for 1212 failures in a few minutes is a brute-force or credential-stuffing pattern. The next questions an analyst asks: did the same IP ever get a 200 on /login, and when did it first appear? Both are one grep away (grep 203.0.113.45 access.log | grep ' 200$'). The pipeline gives you a lead, not a verdict. Check whether the address is a known scanner, a corporate VPN exit, or a legitimate user stuck behind a misconfigured client before you recommend blocking anything.

sections.heading: Finding files, history, completion, and chaining commands
sections.content:
### find: search by attributes

**find** walks a directory tree and tests each entry. Its syntax is find where tests actions:

```bash
find /home -name '*.sh'
find . -iname 'passwords*' -type f
find /var/tmp -type f -mtime -1
find . -type f -size +50M
find /srv -maxdepth 2 -type d
```

- **-name** matches the filename against a glob (quote it!); **-iname** ignores case.
- **-type** f for files, d for directories, l for symlinks.
- **-mtime n** tests modification in days: -1 means within the last 24 hours, +7 means more than 7 days ago. **-mmin -30** uses minutes, which is better when something happened half an hour ago.
- **-size +50M** means larger than 50 megabytes; -50M means smaller.
- **-maxdepth** limits how deep to look.

By default find prints matches. Add **-exec command {} +** to run a command on the results, for example find . -name '*.log' -exec grep -l Failed {} +. Always add 2>/dev/null when searching broad areas as a normal user to hide permission errors.

**locate** is the fast alternative. It searches a prebuilt database (refreshed by updatedb, usually daily), so it answers instantly, but it can be stale: a file created ten minutes ago will not appear. Use find when you need current truth or attribute filters.

### History and tab completion

Bash remembers what you typed. **history** lists it with numbers, and these shortcuts save enormous time:

- **Up/Down arrows** step through earlier commands.
- **Ctrl-R** starts a reverse search: type part of an earlier command and press Ctrl-R again to cycle.
- **!!** repeats the last command; sudo !! is the classic when you forgot sudo.
- **!$** is the last argument of the previous command.
- **Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E** jump to the start or end of the line; **Ctrl-U** clears to the start; **Ctrl-L** clears the screen; **Ctrl-C** aborts a running command.

**Tab completion** finishes command names, file paths and options. One Tab completes when unambiguous; two Tabs list the candidates. Beyond speed, it prevents typos in paths, which makes it a safety tool.

History is written to ~/.bash_history when the shell exits, so it is a useful but incomplete timeline.

### Chaining commands

You can put several commands on one line:

| Operator | Runs the next command | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ; | Always, regardless of the result | date ; uptime |
| && | Only if the previous succeeded (exit status 0) | mkdir out && cd out |
| \|\| | Only if the previous failed | grep -q root /etc/passwd \|\| echo missing |

This is where exit status pays off. cp -r data backup && rm -rf data deletes the original only if the copy succeeded. With a semicolon, the deletion would run even after a failed copy, and you would lose both. A common idiom is test && success-action || failure-action, but be careful: if the success action itself fails, the failure branch also runs.

quiz.question: You run the command sort ips.txt > ips.txt to deduplicate and order a list of suspicious IP addresses. What is the result?

options.label: The file is replaced by a sorted version of its original contents
The file is left unchanged because sort refuses to write to its own input
The file ends up empty, because the shell truncates it before sort reads it
The sorted lines are appended after the original lines

quiz.explanation: The shell opens ips.txt for writing with > and truncates it to zero length before sort even starts, so sort reads an empty file and you lose the data. The idea that the file is replaced by a sorted version is wrong because the read happens after the truncation. sort has no protection that refuses to write to its own input when you use shell redirection (only sort -o is designed for that). Appending would require >>, and even then it would not be a sorted replacement.

quiz.question: A teammate shows you this pipeline for counting failed-login source IPs: grep ' 401$' access.log | cut -d' ' -f2 | uniq -c | sort -rn. The counts look wrong, with the same IP appearing several times in the output. What is the fix?

options.label: Replace cut with awk, because cut cannot extract IP addresses
Add the -i flag to grep so it ignores case
Insert sort before uniq -c, because uniq only collapses adjacent duplicate lines
Use sort -n after uniq -c instead of sort -rn

quiz.explanation: uniq only merges identical lines that are next to each other, so unsorted input produces repeated IPs with partial counts; sorting first groups identical addresses together. Replacing cut with awk is unnecessary since cut extracts a delimiter-separated column fine. Case-insensitive grep has no effect on numeric status codes and IPs. Changing the final sort to -n would remove the reverse ordering and would not fix the duplicates, which are created earlier in the pipeline.

quiz.question: You want all output of a build script, including error messages, saved into build.log. Which command does that?

options.label: ./build.sh > build.log 2>&1
./build.sh 2>&1 > build.log
./build.sh | build.log
./build.sh < build.log

quiz.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right: first stdout goes to build.log, then 2>&1 points stderr at the same place. The reversed order sends stderr to wherever stdout currently points (the screen) before stdout moves to the file, so errors still print on screen. Piping into build.log tries to run build.log as a command, which is not a redirection. The < operator feeds the file in as input rather than capturing output.

quiz.question: In an empty directory you run ls *.xyz and bash reports: ls: cannot access '*.xyz': No such file or directory. What does this tell you about how globbing works?

options.label: ls expands the asterisk itself and found no matches in its own search
The asterisk is a regular expression that ls failed to compile
Brace expansion ran first and produced an invalid name
The shell expands globs before the command runs, and with no matches it passes the pattern through literally

quiz.explanation: Globbing is done by the shell, not by ls. When a pattern matches nothing, bash leaves it unchanged, so ls receives the literal name *.xyz and reports that no such file exists. The claim that ls expands the asterisk is wrong because the command never sees an unexpanded pattern when matches exist. A glob is not a regular expression, and nothing is being compiled. Brace expansion uses curly braces, which are absent from this command.

quiz.question: You want to remove the original directory data only after a successful copy to backup. Which command line is the safest?

options.label: cp -r data backup ; rm -rf data
cp -r data backup && rm -rf data
cp -r data backup || rm -rf data
rm -rf data & cp -r data backup

quiz.explanation: The && operator runs rm only if cp exits with status 0, so a failed copy (disk full, typo, permissions) leaves the original intact. The semicolon version runs rm -rf regardless of the copy result, which can destroy both copies. The || version deletes the original precisely when the copy failed, the opposite of what you want. The last version starts deleting in the background while the copy is still reading the same files.
